claims.text: An ML surrogate can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior for hierarchically structured HfNbTiVAl10.
Training on extensive experimental datasets can enable prediction of HEA mechanical properties.
Including hierarchical microstructural descriptors will improve prediction for HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate will run approximately ten times faster than detailed finite-element or atomistic simulations.
At room temperature, its predictions will have errors below 15%.
At 600–800 °C, its predictions will have errors below 20%.
Surrogate-model yield-strength predictions are more accurate at room temperature than at 600 or 800 °C.
The fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 has controlled and reproducible grain size, phase distribution, and other hierarchical microstructural details.
The proposed model integrates elemental composition, processing history, and hierarchical microstructural features.
The model uses advanced feature-correlation techniques.
Grain-boundary density, phase composition and distribution, and defect structures obtained from imaging and compositional analysis are key model inputs.
Experimental HEA data contain correlations among chemistry, processing, microstructure, and mechanical properties.
ML can identify complex patterns in extensive materials datasets and predict properties from input features.
Hierarchical microstructural heterogeneity influences dislocation movement in HfNbTiVAl10.
The model can map microstructural heterogeneity to bonding-related mechanical behavior.
The model can map microstructural heterogeneity to fracture behavior.
Avoiding computationally intensive finite-element or atomistic simulations is the source of the proposed prediction-speed gain.
The surrogate may fail for microstructures, phase transformations, or element combinations that are poorly represented in the training data.
Testing misalignment or unexpected defect formation may reduce predictive performance.
Errors consistently exceeding 20% across multiple independently tested samples and conditions are declared to falsify the accuracy hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The room-temperature claim requires error below 15%, but the declared falsification rule triggers only when error exceeds 20% consistently. Results between 15% and 20% would violate the stated room-temperature hypothesis without satisfying its declared falsification criterion.
